biomarker_name.evidence_quote: Genera such as Prevotella and Klebsiella were overrepresented in individuals with pHTN or HTN. Faecalibacterium, Oscillibacter, Roseburia, Bifidobacterium, Coprococcus, and Butyrivibrio, which were enriched in healthy controls, declined in pHTN and HTN patients. Endogenous compounds whose levels significantly decreased in pHTN and HTN include phosphatidylserine (PS), lysophosphatidylcholine (LysoPC), lysophosphatidylethanolamine (LysoPE). Endogenous compounds whose levels significantly increased in pHTN and HTN include metabolites such as N-α-acetyl-L-arginine, stearic acid, phosphatidic acid (PA).
biomarker_name.section: Results — pHTN and HTN-associated genera; Metabolic profiling
biomarker_name.notes: Biomarkers include both bacterial taxa and metabolites identified as significantly altered in pre-hypertensive and hypertensive patients compared to controls.

biomarker_unit.evidence_quote: The relative abundance of gut microbes was calculated. The relative amount of 26 endogenous compounds concurrently varied in both pHTN and HTN groups is transformed into Z scores.
biomarker_unit.section: Results — pHTN and HTN-associated genera; Metabolic profiling
biomarker_unit.notes: Units inferred from measurement methodology; genus-level biomarkers reported as relative abundance, metabolite biomarkers as relative amounts or Z-scores.

biomarker_value.notes: Specific numerical values for individual biomarkers are not reported in aggregate form; only qualitative patterns (increased/decreased) and statistical comparisons (P-values) are provided. Study reports relative abundance profiles transformed into Z-scores and fold-change patterns.

value: Cohort: 41 healthy controls, 56 pre-hypertensive subjects, 99 hypertensive patients (n=196 total)
Study population: employees of Kailuan Group Corporation, Tangshan, China
Metagenomic sequencing: shotgun sequencing on Illumina platform, 1211 Gb total, 6.18 ± 1.43 million reads per sample
Blood pressure classification: controls SBP ≤125 mmHg or DBP ≤80 mmHg; pre-hypertension 125<SBP≤139 or 80<DBP≤89 mmHg; hypertension SBP≥140 or DBP≥90 mmHg
Metabolomic analysis: 124 subjects (30 controls, 31 pHTN, 63 HTN) by LC/MS in ES+ and ES− modes
Fecal microbiota transplantation: germ-free mice colonized with human microbiota from 2 HTN and 1 control donor
Disease classifier: random forest model using CAGs + metabolites achieved AUC=0.91 (95% CI 0.75-1) for HTN detection
Exclusion criteria: cancer, heart failure, renal failure, smoking, stroke, peripheral artery disease, chronic inflammatory disease, antibiotic/probiotic use within 8 weeks
BP measurements in transplanted mice: elevated SBP (P=0.018), DBP (P=0.019), MBP (P=0.014) in HTN mice vs controls at 10 weeks post-transplantation
uncurated_metadata.evidence_quote: 196 Chinese individuals: 41 healthy controls, 56 subjects with pHTN, 99 patients with primary HTN. A total of 1211 Gb 125-bp paired-end reads were generated, with an average of 6.18 ± 1.43 (s.d.) million reads per sample. 124 individuals from our study cohort were subjected to metabonomics analysis: 30 healthy controls, 31 pHTNs, 63 patients of HTN. Notably, the HTN mice exhibited significantly higher SBP, DBP, and mean blood pressure (MBP) as compared to controls (P < 0.05).
uncurated_metadata.notes: Key study design, population, and methodology parameters extracted to provide comprehensive context for biomarker findings.

host_species.evidence_quote: 196 Chinese individuals. All the individuals in the present study were from a cohort study among employees of the Kailuan Group Corporation.
host_species.notes: Primary study population is human subjects; fecal transplantation experiments used recipient mice (Mus musculus C57BL/6L), but the biomarker identification and clinical disease phenotype derive from human study.

Paper reports cohort-level data stratified by disease group (healthy controls, pre-hypertension, hypertension, and FMT recipients). No per-sample individual data tables are provided; granularity is subgroup_level.
Age information: Paper does not report age values for human participants; only mentions mice were 8-10 weeks old.
BMI data: Paper states 'no remarkable regularity of bacterial abundance based on BMI, age or gender' but does not provide actual BMI values for any group.
Multiple exclusion criteria applied: cancer, heart failure, renal failure, smoking, stroke, peripheral artery disease, chronic inflammatory disease, antibiotic/probiotic use within 8 weeks.
Human FMT donors (n=3: 2 HTN, 1 control) are described in detail in Supplementary Table S17 but not shown in main paper text.
All hypertension patients were treatment-naive ('newly diagnosed hypertensive patients prior to antihypertensive treatment').
No gender-stratified analysis provided despite mention of discrepant gender ratios between groups.
Batch 2 returned granularity='study_level', differs from batch 0 ('sample_level'); kept batch 0.

The schema field 'biomarker_unit' and 'biomarker_value' appear misaligned for this microbiota/metabolomics study. Biomarkers include both taxonomic identifiers (bacterial genera) and chemical compounds (metabolites), which have different ontological representations and measurement units. The units 'relative abundance' and 'relative amount' are methodological rather than physical units.

No quantitative biomarker values (e.g., fold-changes, absolute concentrations) are reported in a single aggregated table. Values are presented as statistical comparisons (P-values, Z-scores, AUC metrics) or as qualitative patterns (increased/decreased) across subgroups.

The paper reports subgroup-level comparisons (control vs. pre-hypertension vs. hypertension) for most findings, but the schema requests study_level values. Data structure supports subgroup_level granularity, but output was kept at study_level per instruction to report aggregate patterns.

ECOG performance status, tumor size, and overall survival are not relevant to this mechanistic microbiota/hypertension study and should not be included in future schema applications for similar metabolomics/microbiome papers.

Host species inference: Primary study uses human subjects (Homo sapiens); animal transplantation experiments (Mus musculus) are confirmatory mechanism-of-action studies, not primary biomarker discovery.
